maintopic: THE LATE RIGHT HON. SIR CHARLES TUPPER, BART.

speechtext:
Right Hon.' Sir ROBERT BORDEN (Prime Minister) presented the report of the committee appointed to prepare a resolution on the death of the Right Hon. *Sir Charles Tupper, Baronet, G.C.M.G.: This report reads as follows:
Resolved, that the House of Commons of Canada desires to express its deep sense of the loss sustained by the Dominion and the Empire in the death of the late Rt. Hon. Sir Charles -Tupper, Baronet, G.C.M.G., C.B. For many years a commanding figure in the Parliament and Government of this Dominion In the confederation, expansion and development of which he played so great a part, Sir Charles Tupper's name and career will ever be held by Canadians in intimate association with the progress and upbuilding of our country.
Full of years and honours he has passed away, leaving behind him a long and impressive record of public service.
The House of Commons avails itself of this opportunity to record its tribute of respect to the memory of one of its most distinguished members.
Sir ROBERT BORDEN moved, seconded by the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the adoption of the report.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, Sir Charles
Tupper entered public life in the province of Nova Scotia, of which he was a native, just sixty years before 'his lamented death last autumn. For twelve years before Confederation he was a leading and com-

manding figure in that province, and his record and career in that provincial arena was what we might expect from one who displayed the great qualities which characterized him in after years in the wider Federal arena. Under his leadership the province of Nova Scotia entered upon a policy of free public education and of active railway development. His proposal for the union of the Maritime Provinces led to the holding of a conference at Charlottetown, at which delegates from the united provinces of Canada made their presence known, and in that way he directly led up to the great movement which resulted in the founding of this Confederation. For nearly twenty years after Confederation he was a member of the House of Commons; and in that historic building on the Hill, now in mins, his was one of the most commanding figures during all that time. He occupied many and important portfolios, and in 1886, or thereabouts, left the active discharge of political duties in this country to undertake the not less important duties of High Commissioner at London. All those who had an opportunity of knowing his record and his work during that time agree, I am sure, that Canada could have had no more able, no more indefatigable, and no more faithful public servant than Sir Charles Tupper. I came into Parliament when the Government of which he was- Prime Minister was defeated in 1896. I had known him, of course, but not intimately, as a great Nova Scotian, before I entered public life, and I can pay with every sincerity this tribute to his memory. After serving under him for four years, while he was leader of the Opposition from 1896 to 1900, I was impressed and inspired with an even higher appreciation of his great ability, and an even greater admiration of his wonderful qualities than when I first, in the autumn of 1896, as one of his followers, took my seat in the House of Commons. He had splendid qualities. Not only his political friends, but his political opponents admired and paid tribute to him. He had a magnificent courage which never quailed before any danger, or in the face of any odds. He had a fine optimism. He was a firm believer in every sense in the resources of this Dominion, and in the greatness of its future. His constructive statesmanship was evidenced in the various policies which he advocated for the development and upbuilding of the country. Whatever difference of opinion may have existed with regard to the wisdom of those policies, no difference of opinion could possibly have existed as to his sincere conviction that they were wise policies, or as to the remarkable ability and the wide vision which he displayed in defending them, both in Parliament and in the country. He was undoubtedly a great protagonist, a man who, in the course of his public career delivered and received as many hard blows as any public man in Canada. But those who knew him intimately, not only his political friends, but his political opponents, will agree that, behind the vigour of his attack, behind the strong and earnest effort which he always orought to the advocacy of the policies, which he upheld, there was absolutely no personal bitterness.
I had the privilege of an interview with him in the month of August last; I went to his home in the country, near London, for the purpose of seeing him before I returned to Canada. So far as his physical condition was concerned, he was, of course, very feeble, but I do not remember ever having spoken to him when his mind was clearer, his intellect more vigorous, or when he took a keener interest in the welfare of this Dominion, in its relations to the Empire, and in all that concerned the Empire at large. I spent about an hour with him on that occasion, and I came away inspired by the wonderful interest he displayed in the great events through which we are passing; by the boundless optimums and courage Which still animated him with regard to the conduct otf the wair, with regard to our duty in the war, and with regard to its ultimate outcome.	.
In him passed away the last of the great Canadians who took a^ leading part in laying the splendid foundations of this Dominion. He lived to see its boundaries extended to the gleat oceans on the West and on the North. He lived to see amply fulfilled the prophecies of early days which his far-seeing vision had inspired. At the last, as at the first, he held an abiding faith in the future of his country, and in its great destiny as one of the sister nations of this vast Empire. Among the thousands who followed his mortal remains to their last resting place, I wlafe privileged to be present. Years ago, he marked the spot where after life's fitful fever he should sleep. There in the quiet God's acre, in the suburbs of Halifax, where he desired to he laid at rest, he reposes by the side of her who for more than sixty years was his faithful companion and help-mate.
I trust that in the not distant future, upon Parliament Hill, there will arise a monument worthy of his memory; but.

his most enduring monument will be the splendid record of achievement which commemorates his name in every province of Canada. Upon the tablet above the tomb of the great architect of St. Paul's Cathedral, there is written this inscription, " Si monumentum requiris, circumspice." So of him, one of the greatest founders of our Confederation, this may justly be said; if you seek his monument, look around you and behold all that he wrought for the Canada that he loved so well and served so faithfully.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House of Commons will honour itself, even more than it will honour the memory of Sir Charles Tupper, by testifying in the most solemn manner its appreciation of the many services and arduous labours of one who was in his time, [DOT] and who must remain for all time upon its roll of honour, one of its most illustrious members, one who contributed in no small degree to make Canada what it >s to-day. Sir Charles Tupper was the last survivor of that galaxy of strong and able men whom the Canadian people delight to honour with the name of Fathers of Confederation. Amongst the able men, who in the fall of 1864, assembled in the city of Quebec with the object of finding a basis of union for the then disjointed provinces of British North America, and whose united efforts brought forth the Canadian Confederation, the name of Tupper stands eminent among the most eminent. Fifty years and more have passed since that date, and perhaps now, we are sufficiently removed from those stormy times to be able to frame a correct estimate of the part played by the statesmen of Canada in that intensely dramatic period of our history.
Undoubtedly to George Brown was due the first initiation of Confederation. He it was, who, by his strong and persevering agitation against the unwieldy union of Upper rand Lower Canada, directed the destinies of Canada towards the Confederation of the older provinces of Biitish North America. It seems to me to be equally true that it was Sir George Cartier who first put the idea into shaue when he set upon it the seal of his essentially practical mind, and brought to it the support of the one province which was material to the idea, if the idea was ever to become a fact.
By his talent and ability, Galt lent aid to the movement; still more did he do so by obtaining for it the influential adhesion of the strong minority in the province fSir Robert Borden.]
of Quebec, of which he was the illustrious representative. It was the good fortune of Tilley to be able, almost from the first, to bring his province to support the idea with a minim|um of division and difficulty. Macdonald was the last to come into line. It is of record that for many years he objected to any change in then existing condition of things, and only a few days before the coalition of 1864 he had almost passionately antagonized the very idea of a federal union. But when ho did adopt the principle he became at once the captain and the pilot. It was his master hand that took hold of the helm, met difficulties as they arose, arrived at solutions of unforeseen obstacles, and steadily and unerringly directed the course until port was reached. And what was the part of Tupper? In his day, this question of Confederation antagonized friends and divided foes. Now that we may look upon it in the calm judgment of history, it must be admitted, I think, that Tupper brought to the cause more firm conviction and took more chances than did any one else. It must be remembered that at that time Nova Scotia was completely against him, and that instead of using time and patience to win the province over to the idea of Confederation, he forced it into the union by the doubtful authority of a dying legislature. The grandeur of the idea strongly appealed to his mind, and he would not let pass the opportunity which if missed might not occur again for many years. If he erred at all, he erred- because he loved not wisely but too well. Indeed, in order to understand the action of Sir Charles Tupper at this important juncture in the history of our country, we must remember what was the chief characteristic of the man. In my judgment the chief characteristic of Tupper was courage; courage which no obstacle could down, which rushed to the assault, and which, if repulsed, came back to the combat again and again; courage which battered and hammered, perhaps not always judiciously, but always effectively; courage which never admitted defeat and which in the midst of overwhelming disaster ever maintained the proud carriage of unconquerable defiance. This attribute of oouTage was the dominant feature of his whole public career, and perhaps never shone more prominently than in the manner in w'hOh he entered public life. It had not been his lot to be born to wealth or affluence. The son of a poor Baptist clergyman, he had succeeded by his own efforts in obtaining an education, and winning a

diploma in the medical profession. He was a young practitioner, not known at all outside the precincts of his own town, and hardly known within them, when with splendid audacity he threw himself against one who was the darling of the people, the most potent influence in Norn Soota and, perhaps the brightest impersonation of intellect thlat ever adorned the halls of a legislature in any part of what is now Canada. Joseph Howe was then the member fox Cumberland. In the province of Nova Scotia there is a tradition still extant, transmitted from father to son, and repeated at many firesides, that on one occasion, when Howe had addressed a meeting of his constituents and had brought Ms auditors to a pitch of enthusiasm even greater than that which his magnetic eloquence had ever before elicited, a young man rose from the audience to reply. It is stated that Howe was somewhat surprised and perhaps not a little amused hut at once yielded assent with something like patronizing -condescension. If the was surprised- at first, he had! greater reason for surprise when he listened to the address of his hitherto unknown opponent. He found that in the speech of this young man there was meat and substance which moved the people and which gave cause for reflection and worry. The tradition further has it, that when Howe returned to Halifax he stated to his friends that he had met in Cumberland a young doctor who would he a tower of strength to the Conservatives and a thorn in the -side of the Liberals. The truth of his prediction was soon borne out, even at his own expense. At the elections which followed in 1855 young Tupper came forward against Howe in the county of Cumberland and wrested it from him. Howe at that time was at the zenith of his fame and it may certainly be said of his successful opponent .that no one ever crossed the portals of any legislature through -so wide an entrance. Sir William Johnson was the leader of the Conservatives in Nova Scotia. He was a man of eminent ability, but being far advanced in years and in poor health, was only too glad to rely on the services of a young man of -so much promise. From the day that young Tupper came to the fore in the legislature of Nova Soo-tia he became the guiding spirit of his party and the inspiration of all his followers. Almost from that day his life became associated with the life of Canada, because it was only a few years afterwards, when
he had become premier of his province, that the movement for Confederation was suddenly started. In that movement for Confederation, with all the excitement that it produced, and with all the agitation to which it gave birth, he found a genial field for his great parliamentary ability.
I have s-aid that courage was his -chief characteristic; but it was not 'his only characteristic. His mind had been cast in a broad mould. Whatever question he had to deal with he never approached it from the narrow sphere of- parochial -limitation; on the contrary, he approached it always from the broadest conception it was susceptible of. When I entered this House, more than forty years ago these were the two things which particularly struck me in him. He was then in the prime, of life and in the full maturity.of his powers; he seemed to me the very incarnation of th-e parliamentary athlete, always strong, always ready to accept battle and to give battle. Though often my judgment was against him, in every case I -could not -say that he was animated by anything else than the broadest view of Canadian problems. When Confederation had become an accomplished fact he r-o-se to the front in the broader arena, just as he had taken the first rank in the legislature of his own province. From the day that he first entered the Chamber of the House of Commons, now unfortunately destroyed, his power was at once asserted and at once acknowledged by everybody. He came into the Federal House under the most distressing -circumstances, for in tihe elections of 1867, the first after Confederation, his whole province had gone against him; he alone had succeeded in retaining a seat. His conduct under these circumstances was worthy of all pra-ise. He applied himself with untiring zeal and unselfishness -to the task -of binding the wounds of his province, -and of reconciling the people to the new conditions. At first he met with but indifferent success; the feeling of resentment persistent only to be assuaged by the soothing hand of time. He had not the supreme gift of which Sir John A. Ma-cdonald was pre-eminently the master: ith-at of reconciling conflicting elements and, with the minimum of friction, of bringing them together as if they had always been one.
In this House his name must ever remain -attached to two measures measures very different in character, hut each

of -which brought forth the particular qualities with which he was endowed; I refer to Protection, and the Canadian Pacific railway- This is not the time nor the occasion to discuss Protection as an economic principle, but I think everybody, friend or foe, must admit that the introduction of Protection into Canada was, be it for weal or woe, was due to iSir Charles Tupper. Sir John A. Macdonald, as in the case of Confederation, had at first been rather indifferent and doubtful; Sir Charles Tupper never had a doubt. He it was who first became its advocate in this House, and he it was who carried on the agitation in the country; and in my humble judgment, great as was the personality and prestige of Sir John A. Macdonald, the victory of 1878 was due more to Sir Charles Tupper than to any one else. But it was not he, after all, who introduced the priciple of protection as an actual measure. He had been the champion, but be was not its artisan in this House. That honour was reserved for Sir Leonard Tilley. But if Sir Charles Tupper did not introduce the protective measure in this House, it was -simply because he did not choose to do -so. He might have had the portfolio of -Finance, but he rather chose the portfolio of Public Works, which at that time included railways. With this portfolio! he had the occasion to attach his name to another very great measure, the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway. All parties in this country had been in favour of a transcontinental railway, but no party had taken up the question with anything like serious earnestness until -sir Charles Tupper took it up with all the vigour of his nature. He organized the syndicate which built [DOT]the railway. Thes-e terms were- much criticised as extravagant and yet though we may yet criticise the terms granted the syndicate as extravagant-such was the immensity of the enterprise that it was more than once on the eve of collapse. Nothing daunted the couuatge of Sir Charles Tupper. He never had any doubt of its ultimate success, and it was his good fortune to see all his predictions more than fulfilled. Sir Charles Tupper had reached the zenith of his fame and power in this House when suddenly he withdrew from parliamentary life to accept the High Commissionership in London- The reasons which induced him to that step never were given to the public. But whatever they might have been, we who were his oppon-[ Sir Wilfrid Laurier. ]
ents thought that he had committed a great mistake. Undoubtedly his services in London were honourable and useful to the country, but in my opinion he was more fitted for parliamentary life, and his services to the country would have been still greater had he remained on the floor of this Parliament. Though absent from Ottawa and in far-away London, his heart never deserted the field of his former activities, and whenever there was a battle to be fought he appeared on the scene, and, with his characteristic vigour, was always in the thickest of the fray. Next to Sir John A. Macdonald, he was undoubtedly in his time the most powerful figure in the Conservative party. Indeed, it has always been a mystery to me and to those who sat on this side of the House that Sir Charles Tupper was not sent for when the old chieftain died. He was sent for at last, but then it was too late. The battle was already lost, and notwithstanding the vigour and brilliancy with which he threw himself into- the battle, he could not redeem the fortunes of his party.
The public life of Sir Charles Tupper ended with the elections of 1900, when he had reached the age of almost eighty years. His strong constitution had at last been shaken by a life of arduous labour, and he withdrew to a well earned rest. But though he retired from public life and the seclusion of his family circle, he continued from day to day to follow with passionate interest the fortunes of Canada. In that daily -spectacle h-e had this great , satisfaction, that the correctness of his estimate of th-e resources of this country, when they were still unknown and undeveloped, was abundantly justified. When at last the end came his eyes closed upon a Canada whose population had doubled and more than doubled, whose national revenue had trebled and quadrupled, whose commerce had risen from a comparatively small figure to the billion dollar mark -and -more, whose products in agriculture 'and industry had reacted figures that would have seemed fantastic in the first year of the Union-a Canada whose people were united even to the shedding of their blood in the defence and for the triumph of those principles of freedom and justice which the Fathers of Confederation had1 placed under the segais of Brutish institutions. To say that the life of Sir Charles Tupper was without fault would be to s-ay what cannot be said of any human life. But it must be said, and

Should ever be remembered, that but for the life of Sir Charles Tupper Canada would not be what it is to-day.
Motion of Sir' Robert Borden agreed to.
Sir Robert Borden moved:
That the resolution of condolence on the death of the Rt. Hon. Sir Charles Tupper be communicated to the members of his family on behalf of this House by Mr. Speaker.
Motion agreed to.

Deeply sympathize with you and the Gov-eminent, Parliament and people of Canada in their great loss. People of Great Britain already bound to the Dominion by gratitude, magnificent services to Empire's cause will be yet" more firmly united to Canada by common grief.

With your
permission, Mr. Speaker, I would like to inform my hon. friend the Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) of the contents of a letter which I have received from a certain county in Ontario. I do not care to give any names at the present time. A new battalion is being raised in this county, and my correspondent informs me that subscriptions are being taken up throughout the locality to supply the men with things which it is claimed are necessary, namely: five field kitchens, a motor truck, granite ware for cooking, a mess tent for the soldiers and a mess tent for the officers, signs or markers indicating the battalion to be attached to the coats of the men, and several other small items. I have heard that this is not the first incident of this nature, but that many similar subscriptions have been taken up. In my opinion, all these things should be provided by the Government as part of the equipment of the soldiers. Can my hon. friend give me any information on this matter?
Everything necessary for the soldiers in the field is supplied by the department.

These subscriptions are being asked to supply the soldiers jvith field kitchens, mess tents, signs or markers indicating the battalion, and so on. These seem to be necessities which should be supplied by the Government.

Field kitchens are now supplied by the department. They were not supplied at the beginning of the war, because a great many friends thought they would like to recognize their local battalions by supplying them with field kitchens. These mess tepts are really not necessary. If a battalion is to be in camp for the summer,. there is no reason why it should not have mess tents, but they are not essential for the soldiers' welfare. We supply motor trucks, but many regiments wanted additional trucks of their own and we allowed subscriptions to be taken up for them in a couple of cases, but only in the way I have mentioned.

I would suggest to my hon. friend that whatever he thinks are necessities should be supplied 
by the Government, and that it is bad practice to allow subscriptions to be taken up for whatever is not necessary.

These things are
not taken to the front; they are only allowed for the summer camps.

It
seems apparent that the apprehension which we had as to one of the members of this House, the hon. member for Yarmouth, N.S., Mr. Law, has become a certainty. It was my privilege and my duty, when I spoke in the House on Friday last, to express my very deep regret at the loss which we have all sustained through his death, and also to express the sympathy felt, I know, by all members with the family and friends of Mr. Law in their bereavement. It has been suggested to me that some hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House who did not find the opportunity to pay a tribute to the memory' of Mr. Law on Friday last, would desire the privilege of doing so to-day, and I hope that with the permission of the House they may avail themselves of this opportunity.

maintopic: THE LATE MR. B. B. LAW, M.P.
speechtext:
On behalf of the gentlemen on this side of the House who have been associated in the representation of Nova Scotia in this Parliament with our friend, Mr. Law, who was the only victim among the members of this House in the disaster of Thursday night, I desire to express my thanks to the Prime Minister for the opportunity he has given us to say a word or two in appreciation of our late colleague. Mr. Law was the oldest member of this House in point of service, with the exception of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), from the province from which we come. He was the dean of the representation on this side from the province of Nova Scotia. Speaking as one who had the honour and pleasure of sitting in the Legislature of Nova Scotia with Mr. Law's esteemed father some fifteen or eighteen years ago, I desire to s.ay that those of us who come from that province regard Mr. Bowman Law as a man who among all our number was typical of the business people of Nova Scotia. He represented the constituency of Yarmouth where, in the old days, the merchants built their vessels and sailed them on the seven seas. He was the inheritor of -a business established in those days, which he extended and developed and

was a type of the men who have made Yarmouth one of the principal sea ports of the Dominion of Canada. By diligence in business he had attained a position, not only in his own county but throughout the whole province, which entitled him to the respect and admiration of all of our people for the splendid qualities he possessed in mercantile life. It was typical of the man that the last words he spoke in Parliament were on behalf of the industry, and of the men engaged in that industry, which is foremost in the constituency from which he, came. He was beloved by the plain people in his own constituency and honoured by men of both sides of politics, and so was re-elected to Parliament by increasing majorities and held a commanding position in his county which few men in Parliament have occupied. Every one who knew our honoured friend appreciated how modest he was in regard to the expression of his views. But, modest as he was he was a man not only of great business 'ability but was possessed of other high qualities which would have enabled him to take a place of eminence in public life, had he directed his abilities exclusively or principally along that line. Exceptionally devoted to the views he entertained and a man of the highest principles and ideals, he was recognized by all who were in close association with him as one of the strongest men in the public life of our province. It is a strange thing that to-day, just after we have listened to the panegyrics on the great Nova Scotian who was at one time leader of this House'and Prime 'Minister of the Dominion, and who passed away recently, by a strange coincidence of fate, we are called upon to mourn the loss of one of the members of the present House from the same province who occupied such a conspicuous place in public life, and who was loved and honoured by the people of that province.
In his private life, those of us who were aware of the relations that Mr. Law occupied with his beloved wife and daughter, who came with him to Ottawa on many occasions, know that these were of a character too sacred to touch upon. We know, however, that the blessings of happy association in family life were given him to enjoy in greater measure than to most men.
Dazed by the calamity of Thursday night, it is hard for us to realize that one who was so closely associated with us is gone and that we shall see him no more. It is one of the strange dispensations of Providence that the finger of death should have
touched him in the very midst of his labours. Knowing him as we did we are sure that when the time came for him to go down into the valley, of the shadow of death, when there was forced upon him the realization that for him the end of earthly things had come, he entered confidently within the shadow, and _ he was inspired by the faith which had guided him throughout 'life and with the certainty of a future which can only be given to men who lived as did Bowman Law. He has passed beyond our ken, beyond the reach of human harm or help,
To that vast realm of silence or of joy Where the innumerable dwell;
and he has left to us, who have been associated with him, as friends and as fellow-representatives nothing but the kindest recollections and a memory which will be cherished as long as life shall last. He has left to his constituents a record of devotion to their interests, of unswerving integrity in business and in political life, well worthy of emulation by us all and by those who come after us- Long after the disaster of Thursday last shall have been forgotten, the name of Bowman Law will be cherished in pleasant memory by the men associated with him and by the men and women of Nova Scotia whom he represented so well in this House.

maintopic: THE LATE MR. B. B. LAW, M.P.
speechtext:
I
had the honour and pleasure of Mr. Law's acquaintance for over fifteen years, and 1 esteemed him very much indeed. I counted him one of my best friends and his friendship was one of my most precious possessions. I have nothing to say except to join my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) in expressing my high regard for Mr. Law's character and my great sorrow at his untimely death.

By this means the Immigration Committee believes it may obtain information which will set the current of our thought and action toward the conditions that will follow the war, and which will lead to intelligent means of dealing with them, with some relation to their causes. We are a little behind by way of thinking that we can deal with any new problem by legislation. If we depend upon this method of dealing with the after-war exigencies here, we shall be framing a poor substitute for the patient, constructive and co-operative efforts which the condition demands.
Therefore, in the United States, by the admission of the President of the Chamber of Commerce, John Fahey, they are already facing this problem and trying to remedy it. But the United States' problem is also, in a perhaps even greater degree, Canada's problem. Speaking on the Address at the opening of the session, addressing myself to the leader of the Government, I said:	_
What reliable nation-wide organization does Canada possess to deal with the following gigantic,problems at the close of the war? The replacing of returned troops in suitable occupations, the readjustment of dislocated industrial conditions and the transference of workers from war industries to normal industrial training ; the industrial training and technical equipment of potential citizens to meet the strenuous and fierce competition for industrial and commercial expansion; the handling of the stream of immigration which will set in when peace is concluded; the replacing of interned aliens from concentration camps throughout the country.
It seems to me that in the above words I gave a resume of the situation which will confront us very shortly.
Mr. John Fahey speaks of technical education. I do not intend to dilqte on that subject as I have a motion on the Order Paper which will come up later on, but everyone will admit, with me, that this question of technical' education is more acute to-day than ever before; and if Canada is anxious to play her part in coming world events, the Minister of Labour will have to give effect at an early date to the recommendations contained in the very able report published by the commission two years ago.
In view of the present conditions in Canada and the prospective unemployment, it is very urgent that Labour Bureaus to which I have referred in my motion should be established. I referred a moment ago 
to the concluding words of Lord Shaugh-nessy. The conditions to which he adverted will be intensified tenfold at the close of the war when hundreds of thousands of soldiers return, when factories in Montreal, in Quebec; in Toronto, in Winnipeg and elsewhere cease their war work, and the whole fabric of trade and industry has to be reconstructed without a large reserve of wealth to facilitate the process. Sir, the victory will go to that nation or group of nations which devote their energy and resources to industrial training and organization. All the component parts of the. British Empire will share in that struggle, and all must participate in the strain. Is it too much to ask that we in Canada, who are so much interested in the future of our young country should now take the necessary measures in order to meet the serious situation which may arise after the war?

Why in the course oi his admirable remarks does the hon- member say that victory will be to that nation which does so and so? Why cannot he dwell upon the desirability of developing our own resources and obtaining that balance in which alone is happiness?

I hope my hon. friend will give us the benefit of his views this afternoon. They will be welcome to the House, I am sure. I am only expressing my own views and I will be pleased to hear his. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister, in answer to a question of the Mayor of Montreal, the hon. member for St. Mary, stated that there was less unemployment in Canada during the last year or so.

Less unemployment
during the last year than a year or so ago. Let me tell my hon. friend that I have here the evidence of Mr. Barnes, M.P-, head of the Munitions Workers Commission, who gave a statement to the London Daily News on his return to London from Canada last summer. He used the following language:
And yet it is producing in an intensified form some of the troubles of the Old World.
I have never seen in Great Britain such an acute unemployment problem as has been forced upon my attention during the last three months in Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

When did he
say that?

He said that last summer. I have not the date, but I remember taking notice of the statement when it was published. I quite agree with the right hon. gentleman that with the war industries that have sprung up the question of unemployment is perhaps less acute to-day than it was a year ago, but the object of my motion is to meet the very situation which will be raised when the war will be ended, when thosp temporary industries will be dislocated and thousands and thousands of workers will be thrown on the labour market without any employment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Of course, I do not profess to know the conditions absolutely throughout Canada, but I am sure that during the past four or perhaps five months the representations which have been made to the Government have been with regard to scarcity of labour and not with regard to unemployement.

They may be as regards scarcity of labour for these special war industries, but at all events I do not fully disagree with the right hon. gentleman. I say that the war industries have perhaps settled for the time being the question of unemployment, although there are many hundreds unemployed to be seen in the large centres of Canada to-day. But my motion has for its essential object to bring to the attention of the House and the country the urgency of establishing a clearing house for the labour market, not for to-day but for to-morrow, when thife war will be ended, when the war industries will be dislocated, when the soldiers by hundreds of thousands will be returning from the front, and when the vast flow of immigration will be setting in to the prairies of the West. In that regard Canada is sadly behind other countries just as the United States, admittedly, from what I read a moment ago, is also behind other countries. Why, even such a country as- Spain has a clearing house for labour, and we must not forget that in Canada the condition of unemployment, the condition of the ordinary labourer, whether he is a skilled or an unskilled labourer, is probably more difficult than in other countries, because of the distance between the important centres. Therefore, Sir, a central labour exchange is necessary to bring the unemployed in contact with the employers. For that purpose I believe that a permanent central organization is needed. It is a delusion, I believe, to suppose that all unemployment
will disappear with the return of what we call prosperity or prosperous times. For these reasons: First, in normal times the labour market is being continuously disorganized through the lack of a national policy with regard to immigration, Second, the workers are kept in ignorance of work opportunities at points distant from their places of abode, due to the lack of an adequate system of intelligence regarding employment opportunities throughout their immediate localities and in more remote parts of the country. Third, the labour market is still regarded as an inexhaustible reservoir to be treated much as we have treated traditionally other great national resources. Isolated seasonal trades, lack of training in industrial and manual activities, lack of vocational guidance, and incomplete provision of employment bureaus are some of the continuing causes of unemployment which it is possible to remedy, and which prosperity waves do not obliterate.
A moment ago I was speaking with regard to the unemployed in our large centres. Will you allow me, Mr. Speaker, to draw your attention to the following words which I find in part 1 of the report of the Ontario Commission on Unemployment? I believe that Canada is probably to-day the most favoured farming country in the world; she should attract large numbers of farmers; her destiny is eminently that of a great agricultural country. Yet for the last twenty years or so the urban population has increased at an enormous rate, and has become really a danger to Canada. At page 22, part 1, of the report of the Ontario Commission of Unemployment-
What is the date of that report?

My bon. friend from Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) interrupted me a moment ago. Perhaps I might direct his attention to some of the resolutions which are suggested in this very able report published by the Ontario Commission on the unemployment problem. I may inform him that, much to my surprise, I find my good friend Sir John Willison advocating wider markets as one of the measures which would remedy the situation.

That is all very well coming from people who do not solve the question.
_ Mr. LEMIEUX: This question, Sir, is a nation-wide question. It is a federal, and not a provincial or municipal question. The handling and distribution of immigrants and labour must not be confined to provincial or municipal authorities. By its very importance, it is a nation-wide question. Mr. Philip Snowden, in a letter written on October 27,	1915, speaking of labour
bureaus, said:
I consider that they are absolutely essential to any system of labour organization, and if properly worked they will be a great help and in no way harm the interests of trade union... As a personal opinion I think it is very desirable that such agencies should be set up as soon as possible in Canada. When I was in Canada last year I was amazed to see the private labour bureau and it was quite clear to me that a Government system was a very urgent need.
I suppose he meant that a Dominion Government system was a very urgent need.
The state of industrial affairs in this country and in the colonies after the war will make it even more necessary. If you had Government Labour Exchange then there might be arrangements made between them and our system to the mutual advantage of both sides.
I agree with Mr. Snowden, who is an authority on Labour, that such problems are not provincial nor municipal, but nation-wide; and in this country they must be dealt with by federal authority. Such problems are interprovincial in their character; they can not be adjusted by provinces or by municipalities. The responsibility of solving them rests on the Federal Government, in co-operation, if you please, with the provincial and municipal authorities- Unemployment and the conditions of industry are not merely local problems. They 
involve, in my judgment, the larger unit of the nation. The unemployed must not be left to sporadic organizations, if I may so term them, such as those commercial employment agencies which generally exploit labour. They must not be left to mere chance, or to optimistic reports which are spread abroad. The u'nemployed must find a way'to a central organization, which is defined by all writers who have studied this question as a clearing house for labour.
Nor should we confuse the unemployed with the unemployable. One day in London, just as I was coming from the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council on my way to Charing Cross, I met one of those famous processions of unemployed. They were passing by the thousands, preceded by the policemen of London, who, as we all know, can always maintain law and order. The unemployed were carrying banners with the inscription: " We want work and we want bread." One of my friends of the English Bar said to me:	There are only 25 percent of unemployed in this large procession; rest assured that the other 75 per cent are unemployable. You must not confuse the unemployed with the unemployable. The unemployable-that is, the vagrants, dependents, defectives, inefficients -should be treated by themselves as a problem of ' regeneration, but the unemployed should be looked after by those labour bureaus or clearing houses for labour.
Mr. Speaker, the labour market of this country must be organized, and systematized, and this is the time to organize it. Federal labour bureaus must be established that will centralize all the powers and activities of federal, provincial and municipal bodies. Labour bureaus are not a new institution, although they would be new in our country. Let us take the example which has been given us by other sections of the British Empire. They, are in operation, for instance, in New Zealand; also in Australia and above all in Great Britain. Great Britain, with her network of 430 labour exchanges, covering the whole country from county to county and from city to city, has proved, through statistics issued, the worth of that system, and its ' increasing facilities in dealing with future problems, when the Empire shall be girded wit)i a chain of labour exchanges, playing the leading part in the distribution of population and labour throughout the Empire. Let me give you a few figures, which speak for themselves. In 1910 Great Britain had

82 public exchanges; these by July, 1913, had grown to 430. In 1912, 2,432,000 applications for work and 1,286,000 applications for workers were received, a total of about
1,051,000	positions filled, or 77 per cent of all notified. Ninety-six per cent of all the workers were, found to have repaid fares, advanced by the Government to enable them to reach their positions. In France 162 exchanges have been established since 1910. Germany before the war had 323 exchanges; in 1911, 1,055,000 positions had been filled through the medium of those clearinghouses in Germany.
I said a moment ago that in the United States they were trying to meet the situation which will arise after the war. The experience of the United States in this connection has been a failure. Their experience is a warning to us as to what conditions should be averted in Canada. Sporadic attempts have been made, through the -establishment of 13 state labour bureaus and 12 municipal bureaus, to deal with national and complex problems. These halting, ineffective attempts have been seriously crippled by insufficient appropriations, lack of prompt interchange of reliable information, lack of proper transportation, little or no intelligent public opinion and active co-operation in maturing and administering the labour bureaus and, last but not least, inferior, incapable officials. Let us take a lesson from the errors made in the United States.
I understand that in 1914 two delegations met the hon. Minister of Labour in connection with this very question. Several organizations were included in these delegations. Five provincial premiers, the Alberta Legislature in Committee, the Agricultural and Colonization Committee of the House of Commons, the Labour Committee of the " Senate, associated boards of trade for Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, affiliated boards of Trade for British Columbia, Union of Alberta Municipalities, Union of Saskatchewan Municipalities, Dominion Trades and Labour Congress president, Canadian Federation of Labour, Canadian Lumbermen's Association, and many others, were received on two different occasions by my hon. friend. The delegations urged the establishment of a public labour bureau system under federal management. This system of federal bureaus has been endorsed by several large and important organizations in Canada. On June 5, 1914, a letter was written to the hon. minister explaining the objects of the labour bureau, which were stated to be: to ameliorate existing unemployment and to provide practical remedies
against its recurrence; to provide for the intelligent and efficient distribution of labour; to provide a substitute for the present unsatisfactory and in many cases fraudulent and unscrupulous practice's of commercial employment agents. In reply to the delegation of May 18, 1914, the hon. minister said, I am told, that on account of the lateness of the day the promised Bill could not well be introduced until the next session, but that the subject would receive very careful consideration not only from himself but from other members of the Cabinet as well; and that its importance was fully recognized. The letter to which I have referred was signed by the president of the Devonian Society, by the president of the Orangemen's Society, the Ottawa Builders Exchange, St. George's Society, Overseas Club, Sons of England, Dominion Trades and Labour Congress, Ottawa Board of Trade, St. Jean Baptiste Society, Social Service Congress, Ontario Provincial Builders' Exchange, originator Canadian labour bureaus movement, United Protestant Societies of Canada. The Ottawa Journal of May 20, 1914, gives a summary of the answer then given by the hon. minister, as follows:
The distances in Canada render it impossible for the Government to advance travelling expenses
Travelling expenses are advanced in Great Britain and other countries. The Journal goes on to say:
But the minister believes that he'has arrived at a solution of the difficulty by getting employers to advance the money. The Minister of Labour has found that to allow persons out of work, especially immigrants, to get into the hands of employment agents has not been in the best interests of the workmen. He found, after going carefully into the matter, that one employment agent in Montreal had made $10,000 in three months out of immigrants alone, charging them as high as $15 and $16 to get them a job.
He has stopped this extortion by compelling agents to take out a government license, and there is now a regular system of inspection.
Mr. Crothers intends to go still further, and will establish Government bureaus at a number of centres of population. Accurate information regarding labour conditions in the various parts of the country will be available at each office, and to these offices those who desire employment will go. Employers also will be able to secure information as to the ability and record of those whom the bureau will recommend to them.
So this question is not new to my hon. friend the Minister of Labour or the Government. Delegations have been received and promises have been made. I do not wish to accuse my hon. friend of lack of diligence ox attention, but at all events the

bald fact remains that nothing has been done.
On the 16th December, 1915, the Bound Table Conference at Montreal was called by His Lordship Bishop Farthing, of the Anglican Church, and'several of the leading citizens of the metropolis were present, also delegates from the various public bodies, both lay and clerical. The conference adopted unanimously the two following resolutions:
1.	That this conference recognizes the necessity for immediate national action to cope with new and complex conditions arising after the war, and emphasizes the urgent need for a system of National Labour Bureaus.
2.	That a deputation be appointed from this conference to urge upon the Government the immediate establishment of a National Labour Bureau system, with power to co-operate with representatives of other cities throughout the Dominion.
I understand that the delegation above referred to was to meet my hon. friend this very day, but that in view of the catastrophe of last Thursday its reception has been postponed for 'a few days.
I know, however, that a petition has already been forwarded to the Governor-General in Council, the conclusions of which embody a system of Labour Bureau®. I do not know whether my honourable friend has taken cognizance of that petition, and in case he has not I beg leave to read its conclusions :
Therefore we respectfully beg to suggest:
1. That legislation be enacted by the Government this session, providing for a permanent commission, who will be responsible to Parliament to organize and establish a system of labour bureaus for Canada. The salient points to be:
(a)	A commission or authority at Ottawa with executive power over the whole of the Dominion.
(b)	In the chief municipalities a small local Board representative of the local council, of the employers and of labour with power in agricultural districts to co-operate, a representative of a farmer's association-with the agent of the central authority acting as secretary.
(c)	A strict neutrality on the part of the bureaus m the case of lockouts and strikes.
(d)	^ Co-operation with the educational authorities for the better industrial and vocational training of children.	.
(e)	Co-operation with all the Government departments working towards the control and direction of immigration and labour, particularly the post office in the franking of let-' ters and the distribution of bureau literature.
(f)	The officers appointed to carry out the system to be tested as to business efficiency and vocational fitness by a board of examiners.
(g)	Where necessary, separate waiting rooms shall be provided for men and women, with proper supervision.
(h)	Owing to the number of women engaged in industry, it is recommended that a woman

be a member of the commission and local boards.
2. That your Government take such steps as they, in their wisdom, may deem expedient, m order that some immediate action be taken to ameliorate our present conditions, and with greater efficiency and success meet the new conditions arising after the war.
This petition, and the resolution unanimously passed at the Bound Table Conference on the 16th of December, 19X5, - weTe endorsed by the Montreal Board of Trade at their last sitting. The prayer of the petition, which was endorsed, is as follows:
That legislation be enacted by the Government this session, providing for a permanent commission, who will be responsible to Parliament to organize and establish a system of labour bureaus for Canada.
I stated at the beginning pf my remarks that the problem this country would have to face to-morrow is threefold: first, replacing our returned soldiers in civilian employment; second, the consequence of the displacement of the munition workers to the extent of at least over one hundred thousand; and third, a very large influx of immigration. Each of these three problems requires much thought and study, but I think that the salient points which are to be found in such a system of National Labour Bureaus as I have mentioned will be adequate to solving them all. The salient points are:
1.	A Commission or authority at Ottawa with executive power over the whole of Canada.
2.	In every municipality or district a small local board, representative of local council, labour and trade.
3.	Wherever possible, the present machinery to be used and the co-operation of the Provincial Governments invited.
4.	A strict neutrality on. the part of the Bureaus in the case of strikes and lockouts.
Such are the chief features of the system the establishment of which I strongly advocate. I repeat that I thoroughly re-echo the sentiments that were expressed at the round table conference held at Montreal in December last. I believe this question is a vital one, involving our future as a nation, and that it is one which should, be take'll into very serious consideration by the Government of the day. The war has created new conditions; let us be ready for its aftermath.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. W. CEOTHERS (Minister of Labour):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad that my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. FEBRUARY 7, 1916 '
Lemieux) has brought this subject to the attention of the House. The hon. gentleman has had a good deal of experience, having been closely connected with the Department of Labour when he was a member of the late Government, and his judgment on a question such as is being discussed this afternoon is therefore of considerable value. I am also glad, because it gives me the opportunity of correcting some misapprehensions that exist concerning this question of the establishment of labour bureaus.
My hon. friend has referred to some delegations that waited upon me some two years ago. I think there were five delegations altogether. They were all inspired by the same individual, who had a personal object in view. He desired a position under this Government at a large salary. The same individual, I am advised, many and many a time waited upon my hon. friend when he was in the late Government, and also upon my predecessor in this office, pressing upon them the advisability of establishing such a system of labour exchanges as my hon. friend has advocated to-day. I do not know whether L should congratulate my hon. friend upon having changed his opinion - since he was in office, and when he had the power of granting the request made by this individual. At any rate, he did not grant the request. It does not appear to have struck him and my predecessor so favourably when they were in power and in a position to grant such a system of labour exchanges.
My hon. friend from Rouville has referred to conditions in Germany, Great Britain and Australia. It is very often said that there is in Australia a federal system of labour exchanges, but such is not the case. The Commonwealth of Australia has made no enactments whatever for the establishment of labour bureaus, but I believe that two or three of the separate states have. In Great Britain and Germany, where there are systems of labour exchanges, they are coupled up with a national system of unemployment insurance, sickness funds, and several other provisions for the amelioration of the condition of the working people. While I do not speak with certainty, I think that these matters are within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures, and not within the jurisdiction of the Federal Parliament.
My hon. friend has also referred to conditions in the United (States. In the year 1907 the United States established a system
of labour bureaus, although it is not a perfect one, as my hon. friend has stated. During the last eight years, according to a report recently made, they have provided positions for about 40,000 men. We have in this country an agency at work which, during the same number of years, although we have a population of only eight millions as against ninety odd millions in the Upited States, has provided positions for about
130.000	men. My hon. friend is aware that the Immigration Department of this 'Government has for years been engaged to a large extent in providing positions on the land for the unemployed who desire work, and beginning with the year 1907, when the late Government was in power, the positions furnished have averaged1 about
16.000	a year, excluding the excursions that go out to the West every year to assist in harvesting.
My hon. friend has referred to the conditions which will exist when this war is ended. While I think it is right that we should begin now to think about those conditions, there is no certainty whatever that there will be anything like the immigration about which my hon. friend speaks almost with certainty, and I do not think it is wise at present to arrange by legislation for conditions which may not exist at the close of the war. We are taking steps in that direction not only for the soldiers who return invalided, but for those who will return when the war is over. My hon. friend knows that a Military Hospitals Commission, under the presidency of Senator Lougheed, was established by this Government some months ago. A conference of the Premiers or other representatives of the various provinces was held at Ottawa, and all the provinces were represented with the exception of British Columbia, from which- we received a letter explaining why no representative could be sent. These representatives held a separate conference, the result of which was that they offered to undertake the work of securing employment for disabled soldiers. Since then, as I understand, a provincial commission has been appointed in each of the provinces, and these commissions in turn have appointed local committees. For instance, there is a commission in'the province of Ontario, and I had a little experience of a local committee appointed under that commission in my own city of St. Thomas. The local committee is instructed to meet disabled soldiers at the station on their return, and it provides comforts for them in the meantime,

and undertakes as far as possible to find employment for them. The problem is a very difficult one, as hon. members can understand.
That is for soldiers who are invalided home?

Yes. The Government has shown its keen appreciation of the importance of these matters by referring them for definite consideration and action to the Military Hospitals Commission, called specially into existence- for the purpose, which, under the chairmanship of Senator Lougheed, has already met in conference the Prime Ministers and other representatives of the various Provincial Governments and is arranging a carefully considered plan whereby the Dominion Government, the provinces, and the municipalities will be enabled to work effectively together in discharging the debt which the country should honourably pay to the men who have risked their lives in the defence of the Empire.
It has not been overlooked that the conclusion of the war may give rise to other economic problems in 'Canada, plans to meet which may well be in course of prepartion at the present time, and the Government has created a body known as the Economic Commission, which, again under the chairmanship of Senator Lougheed, is giving careful consideration to, those matters with a view to advising, how best this Dominion may be enabled to meet economic emer* gencies.

What is the principal
object of this Economic Commission? Is it to meet such contingencies as that of the dislocation of war industries, when the war is ended?

The Order in Council appointing this commission sets forth fully the different branches of work they are to engage in. One, for instance, is immigration; another is settlement on the land; another is taking care of the soldiers when they return at the end of the war. I have not it under my hand, but if I can procure a copy for my hon. friend, I have no doubt he will read it with interest.
Has it been laid on the table of the House?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It was laid on the table the Monday after the House met.

The commission is gathering from many sources important in-

formation and expert advice, and it will be better able to frame a conclusion when this portion of its work is completed. In addition to the work the immigration offices are doing throughout the country, locating on an average 16,000 men a year, as compared with an average of 5,000 in the United States under their system, some of our provinces have already established labour bureaus. They have not gone into it very thoroughly yet, but if my hon. friend has read the report of the commission appointed by the Government of Ontario to inquire into the question of unemployment, he will remember that they recommend a system of provincial labour exchanges. They indicate hope that at some future time, when the various provinces have established similar exchanges, the whole may be linked up, with Ottawa as a sort of clearing-house.
My hon. friend has referred to statements of an officer of the Trades and Labour Council, who was present at one of the delegations referred to, but if he will consult that gentleman I think he will find that he is not in favour of those bureaus at-all. The Trades and Labour Congress passed a resolution at its last annual meeting; and if I remember well, they passed a similar resolution at their previous convention, not saying in so many words that they were opposed to a national system or to a provincial system of bureaus, but declaring that they were in favour merely of a municipal system of labour exchanges.

I was not present when the delegation waited upon the Government two years ago, but I was present the other day at a meeting in Montreal of the Montreal Trades and Labour Council, at which a representative of the Dominion Trades and Labour Congress, Mr. Foster, was present, and that gentleman gave support to the proposal I have read.
MJr. CROTHERS: He is only one member; but the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, when it met last summer at Vancouver, and the year before, when it met at St. John, passed a resolution in favour of municipal labour exchanges. I know Mr. Foster very well; he resides in Montreal, and is a member of the Trades and Labour Council there. But the Trades and Labour-Congress of Canada, perhaps the largest body of wage-earners in the Dominion, is opposed to a national-system of labour exchanges.
I was pointing out that the Dominion immigration offices are locating about three

times as many workers, with a population of eight millions, as the system in operation in the United States is locating with a population of a hundred millions. We have some labour exchanges established in the various provinces. They are not very completely at work yet. We have municipal exchanges in several places, and we also have a large number of private exchanges.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

When the House rose at six o'clock, I had referred to some of our facilities for the distribution of labour. I had pointed out that our immigration officials last year had placed 17,250 labourers, and that in the year 1914 they had placed 17,350; that something had been done in the way of developing provincial labour exchanges, and that the prospects were that there would be a very much greater development in the near future; that we have municipal bureaus that are doing a good deal in this direction; that the Trades and Labour Congress favour municipal bureaus and not provincial or Dominion bureaus; that under our system of distribution of labour, a very much larger number of labourers have been placed during the last eight years, in fact, three times as many, as have been placed in the United States under a system which they adopted in 1907. Undoubtedly there is much valuable work to be done in coordinating and systematizing the work of these agencies. This, however, is a work which falls in the first place on the provincial authorities, under whose authority these agencies have been established and are or may be licensed, inspected and regulated. The Dominion Government seeks opportunities of co-operating to the same end, and from this point of view availed itself three years ago of its powers under the Dominion Immigration Act to bring private employment agencies under a system of Dominion inspection, in so far as the agencies might deal with immigrants. This action was taken because of cases which had come to light, in which immigrants had been victimized by these agencies. Enforcement of the new regulation is believed to have worked very effectively for the protection of immigrants. Otherwise the agencies remain subject to provincial control.
There are besides numerous agencies of a voluntary or semi-philanthropic nature, such as the employment bureaus of the Y.M.C.A., Y.W.O.A., Salvation Army, etc.
The Department of Labour, though not exercising or claiming any jurisdiction over these various classes of labour exchanges, is endeavouring gradually to establish a system by which monthly reports are secured from them,- the results of which are tabulated and printed from month to month in the Labour Gazette. For instance, for the month of November last, nine employment bureaus, provincial or municipal, reported 4,668 vacancies notified and 3,782 persons placed; twelve Salvation Army labour bureaus reported the distribution of 1,402 casual jobs to 890 persons,, and Y.W.C.A. officers reported 1,217 vacancies notified and 253 women and girls placed. It is hoped to develop this system of reporting, and it is not impossible that, by keeping in this way and otherwise closely in touch with labour distribution agencies, opportunities may. be found where the facilities of the federal authorities may be advantageously exercised. While, however, there is apparent advantage in the coordination, so far as may be possible, of the various and numerous classes of agencies now working to the same end, there is perhaps some ground for the view that the assumption by the Dominion of practically all responsibility with reference to the-distribution of labour, in the manner suggested in many published statements on this subject, would lead to a cessation of the excellent work resulting from existing enterprises, particularly those of provincial and municipal bureaus.
In conclusion, it may be said that unemployment is less at the present time than normally; existing facilities in labour distribution are large and of a nature permitting extension as occasion requires. The Government is not unmindful that the future may bring emergencies, means to meet which are a matter of careful and immediate consideration.
The hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) spoke of unemployment. There is practically no unemployment in Canada to-day. Many employers are looking for labourers and are unable to find them in as large numbers as they desire. In the respect things are very different from what they were fifteen months ago. About a year or fifteen months ago there was greater activity in the direction of efforts to establish these labour exchanges than

there is now. One can easily see that with conditions as they were fifteen months ago, that is with a surplus of labour everywhere, so that there was no place where you could direct one hundred men to go and find work, these labour bureaus would be of no use; and, when there is a scarcity of labour you do not need any labour exchanges. To-day no man who is able and willing to work need he idle-and that is to a large extent the case at all times. There are exceptions, but as a rule the man who is out of work does not want to work. We had some. experience of that kind in Ottawa a year ago, when we had sixty-four bona fide applications from farmers in the Ottawa valley for men to go out and work on the farms, yet during the whole winter we could only find fifteen men who would go to fill sixty-four,places. There were scores of men going to the city hall every morning to get a loaf of bread, but they would not go out to work for the farmers at $20 a month and their board. I know of a case where a man offered to hire fifty men out of work and to give them $20 a month and board and lodgings. But they said: No, we prefer to remain here and to go to the city hall every morning and get a loaf of bread to working on a farm for $20 a month and our board. My hon. friend referred to the problem of getting men on the land at the close of the wa!r- We will have an opportunity to discuss that on another motion to be proposed by the hon. gentleman. But it seems to me, that the important problem that will face us when the war is over, will be to get men upon the land where they will cause two bushels to grow where there is only one growing now. That is the effort we shall have to make. We do not want to firing men to this country who will go into the cities, who know nothing about the land and do not want to work on the land. As I have said, our great problem will be to get men upon the land, to make land productive which is not productive now. Of course we have fish and timber and minerals in this country, but I believe that our richest natural resource is the soil and -that it is the duty of the people of Canada to see to it that our great open, vacant spaces are filled up with men who will produce something out of ground that is now producing nothing.
My honourable friend referred to technical education, hut that subject also will be discussed on another motion of my hon-

ourable friend's, so I shall not deal with it now.

Mr. Speaker, as a representative
of labour, organized labour especially, I will say at the outset that we do not want these employment bureaus. There are many reasons for that position, but they are too long, to enumerate. From the information I have gathered from members of the House of Commons in Great Britain, and from other Dominions, this system is not working as well as it it is supposed to be in those parts of the world. We came to the conclusion that it would 'be one of the finest political machines that could be invented fox a political party. Of course it may not be looked upon in that way by all, but I know it could be worked in that way and my honourable friends on both sides of the House know that too.
I wish to speak especially on the question of non-employment and I may say at once that I do not quite agree with the Minister of Labour in respect to non-employment. I will admit that there are fewer men walking the streets to-day than there were a year ago, but we must bear in mind the positions in which many of these men have been placed. A great nrany men who were receiving a living wage prior to fifteen months ago, have had today to accept half a living wage. Many who were working for about $3 per day eighteen months ago are working for $1.75. There is no doubt that the number walking around the streets is less now than it was then, but we must remember that these men have been forced by circumstances which we all appreciate to accept positions altogether inferior, so that they have not now the same power to buy the necessities of life for their families. That is probably why we do not see so many men walking the" streets to-day. We must also bear in mind that great numbers of men 1-eft the country ait the outset of the war, and two and a half or three months afterwards there might have been a sudden shortage in the supply of labour. I have always noticed, in my experience in life, that if employers of labour want men, even for two or three weeks, they have it published in the newspapers all over the country that there is a big shortage of labour. It is not a question of how long they intend to employ those labourers; it is a question of .employing them there and then; it is not a question of what they are going to do after the work, however short

it may be, is over. In the large cities to-day -I know that there are some in Toronto, and also in Montreal-there are men asking every day for positions. They say: can you find me a position, at labouring or anything at all. Of course there are positions in connection with shell making and so on, but I take this occasion to state that if one of those men does not happen to have a recommendation from one who supports the Government he does not get the job.

I would like my hon.
friend to give us some names or some evidence in support of that statement, because I do not think it is a correct statement. The Government are taking no part of any kind or description in the making of shells. I think that is a very unfair statement to make.

I can give my hon.
friend names and places. I am stating exactly what happens. I do not say the Government aTe responsible; I do not know that. I am not accusing the Government when I say that a man who does not have a recommendation from one who supports the Government cannot get a position. I do not say that the Government have given instructions to that effebt.
Give us a case in point.

I will give to my hon. friend privately or publicly, next week if he likes, the names and places. Whether it is the fault of the manager of the works or of some subordinate, I do not know. I am not going into these details now, but I have come to the conclusion that if one of those poor men wants to get a job anywhere he has to see his own member and get a lettter of recommendation. I am merely stating a fact, and my hon. friend will correct me if I am wrong, when I say that there are a certain number of men unemployed in the cities at the present time. It is quite a problem I know. I could never see that it was possible to prevent men from getting positions if the men were really wanted.
This question of unemployment is going to be one of the most acute questions that ever came before any Parliament in any country 'in the world. So far as immigration is concerned, I do not anticipate that we are going to get the very big influx of immigrants that some people expect. That is my personal view. I cannot help wondering how many men will be left in the home land after the war is over. At the present
time there are organized in Britain and also in France institutions to prevent if possible immigration, .because they recognize that after the war everything will have to be reconstructed. Therefore, I do not anticipate the big influx of immigrants that others do. My view is that it is the men at home that we shall have to look to. Industries . connected with construction work have practically ceased operations during the past two and a half years, and the trades connected with construction are the trades that we base our opinions upon. I admit that many of the men who were employed in construction work are now engaged in other industries, such as making shells and munitions of war, but after these industries stop we will have a tremendous number of men out of work. Probably by that time the country may be in a position to provide public works to em-' ploy the greater part of those men; it will probably come to that, 'but it is a very big problem to face.
I want to come back to the question of employment bureaus. Where they are controlled by private individuals, these employment bureaus are' absolutely wrong. My hon. friend the Minister of Labour knows that in the city of Montreal some of the individuals running those private institutions were dragged before the courts for levying exorbitant charges on the men. They used to send the men to places where there were no position^ to fill. I claim that every one of these institutions should be abolished. I have no objection, .and the labour men of this country have no objection-I am speaking now for organized labour-to municipal bureaus if they can work in harmony with the different provinces, because they form a kind of family circle in which the problem can, be handled very much better than by private individuals. We have a municipal bureau and a provincial .bureau in Montreal, and both work in harmony. I can assure you, Sir, that they are not .strike-breaking bureaus. What organized labour fears, and rightly fears, from their experience, is that if those bureaus were established by the Federal Government throughout Canada, it would be an easy matter, four or five or six months before some labour trouble threatened, to send a number of men as strikebreakers.
My hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Le-mieux) made a reference to the attitude of the Trades and Labour Congress. I am sorry to say that he must 'have .been mis-



informed. The president of the Trades and Labour Congress may have said, speaking as an individual, that he "was in favour of employment bureaus, but if 'he made that statement he had no right whatever to speak for organized labour in this country. My hon. friend attended the meeting in Montreal. I was asked to attend that meeting, but I would not go. He attended that meeting, hut he was non-committal. The president of the Trades and Labour 'Congress had no right to commit the labour men in that respect, and I do not suppose he did to the extent which my hon. friend imagined. My hon. friend the Minister of Labour spoke at the different associations that at the present time operate as bureaus,
/ and he mentioned the Salvation Army and other organizations. I would advise the Salvation Army to keep to their spiritual work and not to bother about placing people at work. It would be a great deal better for the working men of this country if they did so, because experience has proved that these people were more interested in getting so much per head some few years ago, if not now, than in where the men were to go. If we -are going to solve this precious problem, if I may -so term it, we shall have to face it in a manly way. The taxes are increasing -and hearing more and more upon every working man, woman and child, and I believe, -as many others believe, that if the taxation was lowered, and the people were afforded wider markets so as to enable them to secure the necessities of life, it would be -a -step towards solving the problem of employment.
Of course, there is a school made up of persons who think they know how to settle this problem altogether. First of all, they say that if we want the staff of life we must own all the mills. But after we obtain ownership of the mills we shall have to own all the fields and grow the wheat ourselves; we shall have to own the bakeries, and everything of that kind. Well, at the present time I do not suppose that any government is ready to go that far. That * is why the liberal-minded men of the country have been always in favour of the nationalization of public utilities; and I believe that that should be the first step. According to the last report of the Minister of Labour, the cost of-living has increased throughout the country; the report, issued,
I believe, in August, showed an increase of about five per cent. That report showed what is would cost the workingman with a salary of $800 do live, taking into account
	t
some 28 articles which it was necessary for him to buy.
