We know that at present there are any number of men who are obliged to accept positions at a much lower wage than they received prior to the breaking out of the war-and the cost of living is still increasing. Rents are increasing, too; though some may say that they are not. What we call the big rents are not increasing, but the economic conditions have forced certain classes of people to move, we will say, to another street, and while formerly they were paying $40 a month, they were forced by economic conditions to move to a street where they should pay $25, but they are paying $27 a month. And a man who lived on that same street and who formerly paid $25 was obliged to move to a section of the city where the rents should $15, but where he pays $17. So you will find that the lower rentals have increased to the extent of two or three dollars a month. Rents, therefore, have decreased for the class of people who can best afford to pay, hut they have increased for those who can least afford to pay.	-
Different associations in Canada to-day, including all sorts of church denominations and benevolent societies, are asking for such a provision as that which is suggested by the hon. member for Rouville, hut they are all asking for something that they do not want, and something that is not wanted by the people who ask for it. True, it is a good thing to bring the matter up and get the decision of the House upon it, so that the people of the country will know once for all what the labour man wants; but if the House passes a measure of that kind they will do it against the will of those who are most interested in the matter.

My apology for making some remarks upon this question is that I have devoted many years to the study of it. I have been very seriously impressed with the fact that whilst nowadays we apply scientific principles to the study of every other subject, to the economic problem we continue to apply all the old haphazard methods that have endured for so -long.
I was much struck with the opening remarks of the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux). He spoke of what he called the industrial victory, saying that if we in Canada were to do in the future as we should, namely, accomplish some wonderful conquest, or obtain some great industrial victory, then we must pre-

zation, luxury, development, or what you will. But this is something that can be handled only by the people themselves, and the people can handle these things only by means of a central organization, and that central organization is their Government. And unless the Government says: this must be done, and that must not be done; unless the Government finds out how all these units may interchange their affinities and activities so that the different -parts of the body of the state may work together in unison and harmony, they have not accomplished the first step in economic science. It is useless, therefore, to talk of bureaus, or benevolent societies, and all these other so-called agencies or remedies for the public good, when the seat of the disease has not been ascertained. And the seat of the disease has not been ascertained, because the seat of its occupation has not been ascertained. As we all know, there was' a time when throughout the world physical disease was treated according to symptoms. Sometimes the symptoms gave certain ideas to the doctor, and if he was a little lucky he might perhaps hit what was the matter and treat it accordingly. By and by a Frenchman discovered, and a German also, that disease proceeded from the deposits of certain germs. When that was ascertained, it was simply a matter of finding the germ and the deposit and applying the neutralizer. That was scientific; the other was guess work, experi-mentalism, empiricism. From that date medicine ceased to be an empirical science, falsely so-called, and became a natural science. Economic science too must be a natural science. It must find the germ of the trouble, and the body in which it lies, and then apply the neutralizer and allow nature to have its full scope. Otherwise there will be no natural development and, consequently, no permanent development. Surely we have seen to be utterly useless the various theories promulgated since the beginning of the world which were in opposition to nature. Nature governs, nature is clearly and admittedly the expression of the will of God. For men to eradicate nature, to set it at naught, is clearly so absurd that at last the world found it out.
Mr. WM. CHISHOLM: Why not try theology on it.

I will come to you in a minute. These things have been found out by scientific men at various times, and until this labour problem is determined in

a similarly scientific manner, there is no possibility and no hope of a solution. Theology is, of course, a little uncertain, but I would expect the hon. gentleman to turn to theology, as it coresponds best with his state of mind, which is somewhat chaotic and decidedly nebulous. I would expect the gentlemen who do not give much thought to these matters and who read less about them, who think what is is, and that what is not ought not to be, to ignore absolutely what stares them in the face, what appears in every magazine, what newspapers even furnish from day to day, what cheap text books enable them to learn; and that is: that the age of those things we have been speaking of has disappeared, and a new age has arrived, and the economic problem must be treated in a new way.
To repeat, before I close. Just as in nature and in all science the aim is to find out what will produce a happy state of rest, satisfaction or equlibrium, so we must strive to find out that which will produce in the economic body known as the industrial portion of the -state that equilibrium, that natural compensation which alone can produce satisfaction. Otherwise we can never hope to attain rest.

I have listened with a good deal of pleasure to the philosophic arguments of my hon. friend from West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham). The hon. gentleman's remarks are always very interesting, but whether his remarks will help us to arrive at a conclusion as to whether or not labour bureaus should be established throughout this country is a question. I remember hearing the question of labour bureaus discussed in this House last year, and I do not intend to make any remark in regard to that phase of the question, except to say that I have always understood that the object of establishing labour bureaus throughout the country is to enable men to go to that portion of the country where they can obtain employment. - If that is the object, I do not see why the system should not be given a trial. I do not think the Minister of Labour can argue against it on the grounds of expense, because, it being a fact that labour bureaus are established in some of the provinces to-day, all that is necessary would be to establish an organization in connection with the Labour Department in Ottawa. This organization could co-operate with the provincial labour bureaus, and in that way the matter of

expense would be reduced to a minimum. Notwithstanding what has been said by the Minister of Labour to-night, I see no valid objection to the establishment of this system for the purpose of distributing labour throughout Canada.
At this point it seems to me only fair to correct an impression that, I think, was left by the honourable member for Maiison-neuve (Mr Verville) in regard to the Salvation Army. Although I do not know under what' conditions the Salvation Army bring immigrants into this country, I know that they have brought many immigrants who have located in western 'Canada-I am not so sure about the East. As regards the organization of the Salvation Army, I know that they have done a great deal in the way of distributing domestic help in the western, cities of Canada and also in finding employment for all kinds and classes of men.
At the present time the question of unemployment is toot very serious in this country. I understand that in the eastern cities no man need go without employment to-day, and that the siame can be sain of Winnipeg and the smaller cities with which I am familiar in the province of Saskatchewan, although I cannot say anything about the cities of Calgary and Edmonton. Before the war the condition of labour was abnormal, in my own city hundreds, and in Winnipeg thousands were out of employment. We all remember that some 9,000 men

if I am exaggerating the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) will correct me-marched to the legislative buildings in the city of Winnipeg demanding employment and other assistance from the then Provincial Government. In the eastern cities of Canada practically the same condition of affairs existed, large numbers of men being out of employment. -Since the war started, by reason of the manufacture of munitions and also because a large number of our unemployed enlisted for overseas service, we have -not had those conditions of unemployment. -I am not however, very optimistic, as to the condition of affairs in Canada after the war is over. I believe that when peace is declared, when the manufacture of munitions in this country ceases and when our soldiers return, we are going to have conditions of unemployment here, although I do not agree with my honourable friend from West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) that for that reason w-e should not bring immigrants into this country.
The Minister of Labour said, in reference to the Military Hospitals Commission, that iMr. W. M. Martin.]
this Government is doing something for the returned soldiers, but I understand that the work of this commission is confined to looking after soldiers who are invalided home. I would not for a moment suggest that the Government is not doing wh'-.t it should in regard to -looking after returned soldiers, but it is not entitled to all the credit with regard to the formation of the Military Hospitals Commission, because if -I am correctly informed, the men who are doing the work in connection with that commission are the local organizations of each province, and I believe, when the various provincial representatives met the representatives of the Dominion Government here some months ago for the purpose of forming this commission, the resolutions were framed and all the work in connection with the organization was done by representatives of the various provinces.

I thought I made it
clear that what the various provinces undertook to do was simply to find work as far as possible for the invalided soldiers and to aid us as far as they could in opening up institutions for the blind and the insane, the Government paying them for any patients who might be taken in. The Military Hoe-pitals Commission provide convalescent hom-e-s of which they are operating a large number now, -and they are also undertaking to re-educate men, and do other work of a similar nature.

I understand that the Dominion Government is paying the cost of all this work, and I am not finding any fault in regard to that. I believe it is better that the work should be handled by the local authorities, because they can get more Teadily into toudh with the men who come back from the front.
Let me refer briefly to an experience of mine in connection with the Military Hospitals Commission, and in doing so I must refer to the 'Militia Department. Some time ago I wrote to the Minister of Militia in regard to three men who returned from the front, one df them being discharged in September, one in October, and one in December. Each of these men had about a hundred dollars coming to him by way of back pay-I have forgotten the figures because my correspondence has been destroyed. Now, I have been trying for the last three or four months, through the city organization of the Military Hospitals Commission, which is looking after the welfare of the returned soldiers, to get this

back pay, but shave failed in my efforts, and these men are depending simply on local charity. It is perhaps not in order to deal with a question of this kind at this stage, but I thought of it when speaking of the Military Hospitals Commission.
Other commissions have been mentioned during the course of this debate. I do not think that I heard the commission with respect to the High Cost of Living mentioned by the Minister of Labour, but that commission went throughout the country; it was in the city of Regina, although the information which it got in that city did not amount to much, because it did not get into touch with the proper people to give it information as to local conditions. So far I have not, seen any report of the work of that commission, and I hope that the Military Hospitals Commission will show better results. The Minister ol Labour also referred to the Economic Commission, the powers of which are wide enough to include almost everything, so that we should expect some results from that august body of men chosen by the Government to look into questions ol economics. I believe, as my hon. friend from West Peterborough has suggested, that this commission will deal with economic questions in a practical manner.
The present Government might very well make use of the valuable reports submitted in a number of volumes by the Commission on Technical Education appointed some years ago by the late Government. When our soldiers return from the front without employment, and some of them without sufficient means of subsistence and without a trade at their back, valuable assistance could be given them if the Dominion Government, in conjunction with the Provincial Governments, would establish some system of technical education whereby these men might be taught some method of making a living.
I wish to refer for a moment to the question of immigration. I do not agree with my hon. friend from West Peterborough when he says that there are too many men on the land, and that that is the reason why farming does not pay.
There is a general impression, and to some extent it is justified, that farming in certain parts of this country does not pay. I can advance very substantial reasons for that condition. The reason is not that there are too many men on the land, but that in the part of the country I come from farmers are too much hedged about by restrictions.
fM. W. M. Martin.!
By the lack of free wheat-perhaps; the Minister of Public Works says: "perhaps." But he knows what the people of western Canada think of free wheat, and if the hon. minister told fully and frankly what he believes on this subject I have no doubt that he would agree with me in favour of free wheat. If I mistake not, the Minister of Public Works at one time almost promised the people of Manitoba free wheat, or some kind of free trade with the nation to the south. But we will deal with that later in the session.
There is another condition which causes farming, perhaps, to be not so profitable as it might be, and that is that the farmer -at any rate the farmer in western Canada-pays a higher rate of interest than is paid in any competing wheat-growing country in the world, and a noticeably higher rate than is paid 'by the manufacturers of eastern Canada. The farmer of western Canada who has any honesty about him at all is just as good a risk for $1,000 as is the manufacturing institution for $100,000 or $1,000,000-and many of these manufacturing concerns get tremendous sums of money from the banks, when the farmers in my part of the country cannot get $1,000. The bankers will say that they give every man credit who deserves it. I know something about business, and, having transacted legal business in western Canada for the last thirteen years, I know something of the business the banks are doing. Though the banks are fair as a rule, there are many instances in whidh they are unfair. They do not take the same risks at all with the western farmer that, they take with the manufacturing plants in eastern Canada. Something must be done if we are to settle the West. Our farming lands are those upon which we must put our immigrants, and not send them into the cities, to which immigration has been drifting for twenty years. We must surround farming in this country with such conditions as to put it on the same basis as the business of .the average business man or merchant. If we cannot do this by means of the business and financial institutions that exist now, then, I submit, the Dominion Government, in co-operation with the provincial governments, must devise a system by which cheap money can be got to the farmers on the prairies of western Canada, to enable them to carry on their business at a reasonable rate of interest. This question has been dealt with in other countries; Aus-

tralia, New Zealand, Russia, Algeria, and France have done something in this line.
Even Bulgaria.
And Ireland.

These countries have
taken up the idea of doing something to keep the people on the land. Take the case of western Canada. If an immigrant goes in and is to establish himself as a farmer, he must have capital. The best immigrant we have in the West is the American farmer, and one great reason is that he has sold his farm in the United States and the money he brings with him. So he has capital with which to establish himself. But it is impossible for a man to go on the land and get a sufficient outfit without capital. I do not think it is beyond the power of the statesmen of the Dominion to devise some system whereby the immigrants who may come to this country after the war is over can be provided with the capital they need, at reasonable rates.

I am sure the House appreciates very much the importance of the question brought to its attention by my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux). Both sides of the "House are most anxious to take any measure, in the public interest, which will assist in preparing for the conditions which will arise at the close of the war. But the hon. gentleman in his resolution makes a definite statement and it is evident from the statement of my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville), and others who are taking part in this "debate, that there is somewhat of a difference of opinion. With the consent of my hon friend from Rouville and of my hon. friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) I would suggest that the resolution be amended to read:
That this House is of the opinion that the Government should carefully consider the advisability of establishing- a system of national labour bureaus to cope with the new conditions arising after the war.
If that is satisfactory to my hon. friends the member for Rouville and the Minister of Labour, I think the House will approve it.

I accept with pleasure
the suggestions -made by the leader of the House (Mr. Rogers) in view of the spirit with which my motion has been received. I am sure the Government and Parliament will do its duty when the
question again comes before the House for its action-

The hon.
member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) has done me the honour to ask me to second his resolution, which I cheerfully do, with the amendment which has been proposed by the Minister of Public Works and accepted by my hon. friend. I am not sure but that the Minister of Public Works would like to have the discussion closed, with a view to going on with other business. It seems to me, however, that the question is not only very important but is well deserving of discussion by the members of this House. It is not often we are afforded an opportunity in this House to discuss these questions of social and economic importance. Not many days are allotted to us for the discussion of private members' business, and especially for the discussion of matters of this character. When these questions do come up we are very likely to he told, as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) has told us in this case, that the Government has appointed a commission, rather putting it to the House that this shows the keen interest the Government is taking in the matter. The Minister of Labour mentioned the Economic Commission which is to make recommendations to the Government as to action to be taken to deal with questions raised by the war. He referred also to the commission to deal with the cases of disabled soldiers. It seems to me the Government ought themselves to bring these questions to the attention of the House, and ought themselves to deal with them. Some time ago, -when the people thought that conditions were ripe for beginning the work of building the Georgian Bay canal to connect the city of Montreal with tlv Great Lakes, so as to make the most direct and shortest waterway from Montreal to Fort William and Port Arthur, and everybody seemed satisfied that the work was -deserving public support, the Minister of Public Works told the House that a commission had been appointed to investigate the whole subject, and thus the matter was shelved.
And so with regard to the question raised by the resolution. The Minister of Labour says there has been a commission appointed to consider the cases of disabled soldiers, and another to consider the whole state of the country, and to recommend something to be done after the war has been concluded. I do submit that the people of this country expect their representatives in

Parliament to deal with these important questions. Parliament is the great council of the nation. The representatives of the people are sent here from all parts of this country., and I think it is their duty to discuss, and I think the Government should take the lead in having discussed, these questions which are of importance to the future of Canada. Therefore, I am glad that my hon. friend has brought this question before the House, and I am glad it has been discussed to the extent it has. I hope the discussion will continue, because it deals not merely with the question to which the hon. member for Rouville devoted the most attention, that is the question of the employment of labour, but it also deals with the whole question of how the people of this country can best prepare to meet, in a satisfactory way, those conditions which will exist in Canada after the war has been concluded. It deals directly with the question of immigration, to which my hon. friend from Kegina (Mr. Martin) has devoted some attention. No subject is more deserving of the attention of this Parliament than that of the best method of settling the public lands of this country, in conjunction, of course, with the different provinces. I quite agree with the Minister of Labour as to that; where I disagree with him is that he does not hold out to us any hope that he or his colleagues are going to take the lead and come before Parliament with some definite and advanced proposition along these lines. My own view is- _ and, while I have entertained that view very strongly for a considerable time, yet 1 have hesitated to advance it because it may not meet with popular approval-but my own opinion is that the day has gone by when our lands should be given away as free homesteads to everybody who chooses to enter upon them and occupy them.
I quite agree with you.

I am glad indeed to hear the Minister of Public Works make that statement.
Mr. W. F. MA'CLEAN: What would you do ?

In conjunction with the different provinces, with a view to promoting immigration and the settlement of our own people upon the 'Crown lands, I would have a careful examination made of the Crown lands in the different parts of the Dominion; I would fix the prices for

those lands at what would be reasonable; I would extend the terms of payment over a long period of time, twenty, thirty, or even forty years; I would make the rate of interest low, and then I would encourage the settler who could be induced to go upon the land. I would- put under cultivation a certain area which would be all ready for him when he went to settle on ' the land; I would build him a house; I would encourage him in the early years of settlement in making a comfortable home. And I would take, in the name of the-Crown, a mortgage on his land and upon his improvements and extend that mortgage over a- long period. Sir, it is in the earlier years of the settler's life upon the land that much of his time is wasted. He becomes heartbroken in many cases and, in many cases having become heartbroken and discouraged, he leaves the land and goes back to the city. Under such a system as I have suggested land which to-day is being given away for nothing would produce to this-country in the course of fifteen or twenty years from $15 to $20 per acre, yielding a small rate of interest in the meantime; and at the end of forty years you would have more money out of the lands than would pay off our national debt three times over. And you would be doing the very best thing possible for the settler because, as I have said, in the earlier years you would be giving him an opportunity to use his labour to the best advantage, to make his land most productive,; and in this way you would be benefiting both the country and the settler by reason of the assistance you would give him, I would re-survey the lands of the West so that instead.of having the'settlers separated from each other by long, distances you could have the settlers in colonies, perhaps with roads running like the spokes of a wheel from a central point which would become the social centre of the community, where you would have the store, the doctor, the church, and the schools and the centres of social life. Thus life upon the prairie would not be so lonely for the settler and especially for the settler's wife and family as it is to-day. This, in a very few words, is the course which I should pursue. But my hon. friend from West Peterborough says: Oh, you do not want immigrants. In reply, I say Canada was never so prosperous as a few years ago when settlers were pouring into this country, not merely by the thousands but by the hundreds of thousands; then the factories of the East

were steadily employed supplying western people, the wholesale merchants weie busy supplying the western retail merchants and the retail merchants were busy selling to the settlers and there was prosperity all around.
My hon. friend refers to one kind of immigration only.

That is the
American system. The credit of the nation is behind it.

No, I think my hon.
friend is wrong.
No.

That was in the Bill
which was passed by Congress last session, but it was vetoed by the President, and the Bill which has been introduced during the present session of Congress leaves out the provision of national credit. There are a good many members of Congress who are in hopes that they will be able to get the Bill changed, so as to have the national credit, hut they very much fear that they will not be able to do so, and some are in favour of accepting the Bill without the national credit provision in it. I think if my hon. friend looks at the Bill he will see that I am correct.

There is provisipn made for large deposits of Government money in this new system of banking. In that way great sums of national money can be issued for the use of the farmers in connection with farm credits. But I see the point my hon. friend is making with regard to improved security.

Will my hon. friends
on the Treasury benches pardon me if I remind them that before the Solicitor General became a member of this Government,
- before he became Solicitor General, he stated to this House that he was in favour of introducing a Bill, and of having it passed by this House, to provide for agricultural credits. There is no one better qualified to draw a Bill along these lines than my hon. friend the Solicitor General. He has become the legal adviser very largely of this Government. He occupies a very prominent position in this House, and no doubt is influential in the Government. But since he has become Solicitor General we have had no word of 'the provision of agricultural credits, no word of the provision of a banking system for the benefit of the farmers. Why is this? Some member of 'the Government might enlighten us, and let us know whether the Solicitor General, who has become a member "of the Privy Council, and therefore a member of the Government, has changed his mind, and whether the Government has abandoned the idea of introducing a Bill along those lines. If the Government has abandoned the idea, and does not intend to submit the matter to Parliament, it will become a question for other members of the House whether they suould press the matter

upon the attention of the Government, and endeavour to rouse public attention in favour of the enactment of such a measure. Of course it will be well understood that a Bill of this nature would have to he introduced by the Government. The most that other members of the House could do would be to agitate for the measure in the hope that the Government would later on see its way to take some action. At all events, if they should not do so during their-they will pardon me for saying it - their short tenure of office.
Smile when you say that.

Then it could be brought to a successful conclusion by their successors.
There are other matters in regard to which this Government ought to ask Parliament to prepare for the future, and to prepare immediately. We should not wait until this war is over. You will agree with me, I am sure, when I say that we should not wait until we have thousands and hundreds of thousands of men coming back from the front, many of them with no work to engage in, many of them who left their occupations to go to the front, and who have no occupation to take up when they return. We should not wait until that day arrives; we should be looking ahead and making preparations. In addition to a broad and comprehensive plan for the settlement of our young men upon our Crown lands, there are surely other lines of industry which ought to receive consideration by the Government. Take the matter which my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries referred to some three or four years ago when he took such a lively interest in such matters. You will remember the occasion, Sir, when he said that he had the smell of the salt air in his nostrils, and that he wanted to assist in the building up of a great ship-building industry. Surely, Sir, we ought not to wait niany years, we ought not to wait until the war is over before we take up that question. To-day there .is a tremendous demand for a mercantile marine in this country, and surely this Canada of ours with its thousands of miles of coast line on the Atlantic and the Pacific, ought to be encouraged by the Government to engage in ship-building. We should proceed with the establishment of a mercantile marine. That would give employment to many people, not to disabled soldiers, but to many people who might want to come to this country, and to many soldiers when they return from the front after the war is over. It would not require 
very much encouragement upon the part of this Government to induce people to establish shipyards upon both the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts. Has the Government thought of this question at all? I fear not, i Sir. I have it from a gentleman in my own city, who would like to take some steps towards the building of sailing vessels with auxiliary engines, that he is met at the very outset with a very heavy handicap. Many sailing vessels which are built in the United States to-day and which are engaged in the Atlantic trade use sails, but they also use the Deisel oil engine as auxiliary power, and they have to pay a duty of something like 35 or 40 per cent on the Deisel oil engine. These engines are not manufactured in Canada, and the man who wants to engage in shipbuilding in this country must pay a duty, as I say, amounting to 35 or 40 per cent before he can bring in the necessary equipment to enable him to build a vessel which, would successfully navigate the ocean. These sailing vessels could be built for a comparatively small sum of money compared with the cost of steel ships. Allow me, with the very best of feeling, to suggest to the Government that they take up this question, give attention to it, and see if they cannot do something to encourage and promote the establishment of shipyards in Canada.
I might go on and speak of many other things which this Government might do, and I beg of them, if anything occurs to them, not to appoint a committee or a commission for the purpose of shelving the question, but to deal with these questions effectively; to submit them to Parliament, to invite discussion upon them. I assure the Government that, so far as the members on this side of the House are concerned- and I believe I can say the same for all the members of this House-any measures which they submit, looking towards the development of any industries in this country, looking toward giving employment to the people of this country and to the additional thousands whom we hope to have before long, will be heartily supported. Proposals on a broad and comprehensive scale will be heartily supported by all the members of this House, and I feel sure by all the people of this country.

The
resolution as proposed originally by the hon. member for Rouville was limited, but there was this to say in favour of it, that it was practical. The hon. member for Rouville evidently had in mind specifically the' matters of immigration and labour

Accordingly, lie ended his resolution with emphasis upon the urgent need for a system of national labour bureaus. At the suggestion of the -hon. Minister of Publio Works, however, the latter paTt of the resolution has been eliminated, and we are left with a pure abstraction. In order to jmake the resolution completely idealistic,
I suggest that it be further -amended to read as follows:
That this House recognizes the necessity Tor immediate national action to cope with new and complex conditions arising during and after the war.
I insert after the word, " arising " the words, " during and,", so that we shall have reference within the resolution to -all the present and future ills which may happen to this country in consequence of the war.
The hon. member for Rouville based his argument this afternoon-I must say I did not follow him throughout the length of his remarks-upon a great immigration into this country after the war. If he or the Minister of Public Works wishes this House to understand' that the new and complex conditions which will arise after the war will be entirely referable to an unusually large immigration, I feel that the resolution is of very little value. I rise chiefly to express in a word or two my views upon the subject of immigration.

My motion has reference not only to immigration after the war, but also to returned soldiers, and to the fact that dislocation will take place in the existing war industries that will throw out of employment -a very large number of workers.

I quite understood the hon. gentleman to discuss the particular which he has just mentioned; nevertheless I heard him distinctly say on more than one occasion during the course of his remarks that we should undoubtedly have a very large immigration into this country after the war. Now, I say it is very important that we have some definite and intelligent view upon the question as to whether or not we shall have a large immigration after the war. If we do not have immigration, then the new and -complex conditions which the resolution states will arise after the war will be of one kind; if we do have immigration, perhaps we may have another set of complex conditions to deal with. The statement has been made frequently by hon. gentlemen in this
House during the present session, as well as by many citizens of this country outside of Parliament, and by many of the newspapers of Canada, that we shall undoubtedly have a very large immigration after the war. As I have already remarked, it is important that we know, so far -as it -is possible to know, what is the future of this country in respect to immigration after the war. I have never yet heard any hon. gentleman in the House or any person outside of the House, give any reasons to justify the opinion that after the war there will be any substantial immigration, or even a -moderate amount of immigration, into Canada. It is quite possible-I think it is quite probable-that for a number of years after the war we shall have practically no immigration into this country. I trust that I -am in error-I am not so entirely pessimistic as to be beyond conviction-but I do -say that those who argue that we are going to have a large amount of immigration into Canada after the war ends should give some reason for the opinion.
The Transcontinental Railway.

I submit -that every -condition rather points to the conclusion that immigration into Canada will be very very -small indeed fox many year-s after the conclusion of the wax. It is not improbable -this is the view held by many men in the United States-that in that part of the North American continent there will be not immigration-, but emigration. I say that the matter of future immigration is a fair matter for inqniry on the part of the Government. It is possible, I think, ito obtain by investigation some facts which will indicate-as to whether the European countries will permit emigration after the war and whether we axe likely to obtain any of it if it comes to this -side of the Atlantic. It is us-eless to predicate public policy upon the probability of a large immigration into Canada after the war unless that probability i-s prima facie established. It would be' a - misdirection of public energy, and, possibly, a misuse of public money, to attempt to provide any remedy for abuses coming from a very large immigration before determining whether we are going to have that immigration or not.
The resolution now-I understand that the Minister of Public Works agrees to my amendment

is -sufficiently wide to enable one to discuss almost -any -matter, and there

are just one or two subjects to which I wish to refer very briefly. One has reference to industrial conditions in portions of Nova Scotia. I have in my mind the county of Cape Breton, wherein are located the collieries of the Dominion Coal Company and the plant of the Dominion Iron and Steel Corporation. There has been >a very creditable and generous enlistment for overseas service on the part of the employees of these two corporations. The enlistments have been tso very heavy that during the past few months, and perhaps at the present time, the operations of these corporations have been very much endangered. The same conditions may prevail in other Canadian industrial centres; they may be applicable to some particular industry in another portion of the country. Notwithstanding the existence of war, this country must pay special attention to production. In order to pay the interest upon our indebtedness, it is necessary to export at least $150,000,000 worth of products a year, and in order to carry on the life of this young nation it is urgent and imperative that the productions of the country be kept to the highest possible level. Just here I wish to say that recruiting should be more directly under the control of the Government than it is. I do not suggest thajt some responsibility should not rest upon the citizens of the country, but I think that recruiting should be controlled to some extent by the Government, particularly in order that enlistment may be discouraged at certain points if the national interest so demands, or controlled in such manner that labour may be transferred from one point to 'another in the event of recruiting weakening the industrial strength of the country at one or more particular .points. This is a matter which, I imagine, may become vary acute in many sections of the country; therefore it is a question deserving the immediate consideration of the Government. The Minister of Labour this afternoon referred to the Hospitals Commission, and the hon. member for Regina (Mr. W. M. Martin) also made a passing reference to it. I am told by those having experience with the duties assigned to this Hospitals-Commission, which is working in conjunction with the Commissions appointed by the Provincial Governments, that the work is not being satisfactorily performed. In my judgment that was likely to be the natural result of control by a Federal commission, particularly a commission of the 
character appointed by the Government. The personnel of that commission consists of very estimable and capable citizens of this country-among the very best people in the country I should think; but they reside in different cities and far apart, and I say it is impossible for this Hospitals Commission properly to do the work assigned to it, and it should be immediately dissolved. A>s the hon. member for Regina has already .stated, the work up to date has in reality been performed by the commissioners appointed by the Provincial Governments, that is, so far as obtaining employment for the men who' have returned from overseas is concerned, and I think that is the only practical work that could have been done by any person. Whether that does or does not include all the work that has been done by the commission, or could be done by the commission, I say that a commission like this, composed of men who reside a considerable distance apart, is not likely to be very successful. I would suggest that there be established under some one of the present departments of the Government, the Department of Militia, or of Labour, a bureau having control of the work which this Hospital Commission is supposed to perform. It would then be possible for the organization in the several provinces to get quickly in communication with the administrative head in Ottawa and have prompt action taken-something which I submit is utterly impossible in the present circumstances. I say-and I am not making this criticism ,in any censorious spirit, or suggesting that, the Government made a grave error of judgment in appointing this commission-but I say that a little experience has proved that the Hospitals Commission as now constituted is utterly impracticable and incapable of doing the work, and it ought therefore to be dissolved.

I just wish to .say a few words on the matter from my point of view. The resolution suggests, and the members who have already spoken on it have also suggested, that now is the time to take into consideration the condition that will exist after the war. I think the resolution has been amended to read " conditions that will arise during and after the war." There is one condition that is certainly going to exist after the war, and that is an enormous public debt, and enormous public taxation, and it would, perhaps, be well to consider whether the country is getting value for the

expenditures it is making, particularly in the Militia Department. We know that in the early days of the war the expenditure was very large, and under the circumstances it probably could not be controlled; but now that conditions are becoming more settled it is a question whether the country is getting full value for the exceedingly large expenditure that is being made. I think all will admit that the Minister of Militia and Defence is not a man who values expenditure. While he may have, and doubtless has, many qualities that fit him for the position he occupies, economy is not one of the hon. gentleman's characteristics. In the system of recruiting throughout the country, for instance, there appears to be no well-defined principle. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) has referred to that to some extent, and I want to mention a few things that have come under my own notice. In the city of Ottawa I see in khaki very old men, some of them seventy years of age I should think. I do not know what military duties . they could perform, nor do I know whether they are drawing pay or not, but I have seen these men on the street, in the hotels, and in the House. Furthermore-I do not wish to be too particular-I have noticed' several members of Parliament dressed in khaki; for instance, the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham), the philosopher, I might call him. I presume he would be able to give good military service. Now, whether these men are drawing double pay or not I do not know, but I say that this is a time for economy, a time when men should not try to make their patriotism pay.
We are asked to consider the condition of the labouring men of this country. We are asked to consider the case of the soldiers who are returning, and who will return in greater numbers after the war is over. But we should also consider the position of the tax payer, who, after all, makes up four-fifths of the population. We know that he will have to bear exceedingly heavy burdens, and we also know as a matter of fact that this war is producing millionaires in Canada. It is producing men who have not only military titles, but titles of distinction, such as knighthoods, which involves a high scale of living. All this is going on at the present time, and it is a serious question whether greater economy could not be practised, greater value received for the money that is being voted so generously by the people of this country for
the conduct of the war. That is a question that might receive consideration now. It is a question that could be considered at any time. It concerns the ordinary taxpayer-the farmer, the fisherman, the miner, the mechanic-the man who is trying to support his family, and who, after all, pays the bulk of the taxes. He has to carry the burdens whatever they be, and the burdens will be heavy, and this country will not again for many years, perhaps forever, be a cheap country to live in. These are conditions that might very well be considered now in order to ensure, as my hon. friend from West Peterborough said, that every man shall give value or an equivalent for that which he receives. We know that this has not been done for the past year and a half; that value has been received for whicn an equivi-lent has not been given. As I already stated, perhaps that could not very well be avoided in the beginning of the great crisis through which we are passing, but it can to a large extent be prevented now provided that the Government tries seriously to prevent it. I thought perhaps I would be justified in presenting this view of the case, because it is of importance and consequence to the class of the community which I represent, that is, the ordinary people, farmers, fishermen, mechanics and men of that class, who have to bear their full share of the burdens that are necessarily being imposed.

Mr. Speaker, having listened to the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. J. J. Hughes), I share the hope which he has expressed, as I understand him, that this country will not become a cheaper country than it is just now, because if ever I heard anything which, to my mind, is a cheap statement to a deliberative assembly, I heard it a few minutes ago when this hon. gentleman presumed to sneer at the members of this House who wear the uniform of His Majesty. I too, Sir, represent a large population of all classes, of the labouring class, of the farming class, of the artisan class, just as good people, I am sure, as those represented in this House by the hon. gentleman (Mr. J. J. Hughes) and who, I feel certain, does not represent his constituents in the sentiments he has uttered here. I will answer the question which he has asked in so sneering a way, as to why some of us are wearing the King's uniform in this House. I can answer it from my own standpoint;

I can tell him that I am wearing the King's uniform, because I heard the call to duty sent out by my King. I read the appeal of the King to the manhood of Canada, and to the manhood of the Empire, to come forward and do their share, and although it is thirty-seven years since 1 first put G-n the King's uniform and thirty-one years since I was privileged before to give field service to the King, I felt that 1 could, without any offence, and least of all without offering offence to the House of Commons, offer my services again to His Majesty. I have the uniform on because I desire to give an example to the younger men of my community, and as evidence that those to whom they look as their natural leaders are prepared to do their part.
I feel sure, Sir, that there is no service which any member of Parliament can give that will be of more value to the military authorities than that he himself should put on the uniform, thus to show to the people of his district, who are invited by this Parliament as well as by the Imperial Parliament, and by the King, to give military service, that their natural leaders, whom they honour with public positions, do not shirk their duty, but are prepared, when the call comes, to put on the King's uniform and render service in the field as well as service in the Parliament of Canada.
Motion, as amended, agreed to.
On motion of Mr. Rogers, the House adjourned at 9.53 p.m.
Tuesday, February 8, 1916.
